content: Iron oxides and oxyhydroxides are a group of compounds with a total of sixteen known variations. These compounds are categorized into oxides, hydroxides, and oxide-hydroxides, each with distinct chemical and physical properties. Oxides: 1. Iron(II) oxide (FeO), also known as wüstite, is a black oxide that, in powdered form, is highly reactive and can ignite easily, posing a risk of explosion. 2. Iron(II,III) oxide (Fe₃O₄), commonly referred to as magnetite, is a mixed-valence compound. In its mineral form, it is also called lodestone and is a significant iron ore. Magnetite forms readily when iron oxidizes in underwater environments, making it commonly found inside tanks or below the waterline of ships. 3. Iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃) exists in two mineral forms: hematite (α-Fe₂O₃) and maghemite (γ-Fe₂O₃). Industrially, it is often called rouge. Purified forms of Fe₂O₃ are used as coatings in magnetic audio and computer media. While it can inhibit rust formation in dry or alkaline environments through passivation, it is also a primary component of rust. Hydroxides: 1. Iron(II) hydroxide (Fe(OH)₂) is a less commonly encountered compound. 2. Iron(III) hydroxide (Fe(OH)₃), also known as bernalite, is another hydroxide form of iron. Oxide-Hydroxides: 1. Goethite (α-FeOOH) is a well-known iron oxyhydroxide. 2. Akaganéite (β-FeOOH) is another structural variant of iron oxyhydroxide. 3. Lepidocrocite (γ-FeOOH) is a third form of iron oxyhydroxide. 4. Feroxyhyte (δ-FeOOH) and ferrihydrite (Fe₅HO₈·4H₂O) are additional oxyhydroxides with unique properties. 5. Other forms include high-pressure FeOOH, schwertmannite, and green rusts. Applications: Iron oxides have diverse applications, particularly in ceramics and pigments. In ceramic glazing, metal oxides, including iron oxides, contribute to the colors of glazes when fired at high temperatures. Iron oxide pigments, such as ochers, have been used historically in art, including prehistoric cave paintings like those at Lascaux. Common paint colors, such as raw and burnt siennas and umbers, are derived from iron oxide pigments. These pigments are also widely used in cosmetics due to their non-toxic, moisture-resistant, and non-bleeding properties. Synthetic production of cosmetic-grade iron oxides ensures the exclusion of impurities and unwanted ferrous or ferric oxides. Typically, Iron(II) oxide pigments are black, while Iron(III) oxide pigments are red or rust-colored. Magnetite, marketed as Black Oxide, is used to coat steel tools, providing corrosion resistance and an aesthetically pleasing finish. Properties: Iron(II) oxide (FeO), or wüstite, is a black powder that is highly reactive and can ignite explosively. Iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃), or ferric oxide, is known as hematite in its alpha form and maghemite in its gamma form. It is used industrially as rouge and in magnetic coatings for audio and computer media. It can inhibit rust in certain environments but is also a major component of rust. Iron(II,III) oxide (Fe₃O₄), or magnetite, is a mixed-valence compound and a major iron ore. It forms readily in underwater oxidation processes and is commonly found in submerged environments, such as inside tanks or below ship waterlines. Iron extraction from magnetite is relatively straightforward compared to other abundant elements like aluminum and titanium.
